Name: harm_prototype_periphery_gap
Title: The Long Tail of Harm: LLM Safety Follows a Prototype Gradient, Refusing Central but Not Peripheral Members of the Same Harm Category
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing prototype theory from cognitive science, we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is governed by a prototype-centered harmfulness manifold: the model reliably refuses PROTOTYPICAL (central, high-frequency) members of a harm category but its refusal probability decays radially with a request's atypicality/distance from the category prototype, even when the peripheral request is equally or more dangerous. This within-category typicality gradient is (1) a distinct, previously-unnamed axis of safety brittleness, (2) mechanistically readable as radially-decaying projection onto a harmfulness direction anchored at category prototypes, and (3) closable by prototype-dispersed representation reshaping that flattens the refusal gradient across the category.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work explains brittleness via (a) shallow/superficial alignment over first tokens (Shallow Safety Alignment 2024; ADA 2025; Incomplete Learning 2025; Markov-chain depth 2025), (b) single/few safety directions, neurons, layers or heads (Refusal is a Single Direction 2024; Safety Neurons 2024; Safety Layers 2024; Just-a-Few-Attention-Heads 2025), and (c) safety-as-null-space-clustering (What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning 2024). Over-refusal work (XSTest, OR-Bench, Self-CD) studies benign-but-alarming prompts. All treat 'harmful' as roughly monolithic within a category and locate WHERE safety lives; none characterize how refusal varies WITHIN a single harm category as a function of typicality/frequency. Our contribution is distinct: we import prototype/typicality theory (Rosch) to advance a graded, category-internal account -- refusal decays radially from harm prototypes -- reframing jailbreak brittleness as a concept-COVERAGE problem rather than a token-depth or direction-suppression problem. This is orthogonal to my prior lexical-vs-semantic proposal (surface words vs meaning): here both prototype and peripheral items are genuinely harmful in meaning; the axis is within-semantic-category typicality. We also derive a novel defense (prototype-dispersed reshaping) that flattens the gradient, unlike depth- or direction-based fixes.
Abstract: Why do aligned LLMs reliably refuse 'how do I build a bomb' yet comply with obscure, equally-dangerous variants of the same threat? We propose that LLM safety inherits a signature of human categorization: prototype structure. Under prototype theory, a category is organized around central, high-frequency exemplars, with membership graded by typicality. We hypothesize that safety alignment learns a prototype-centered harmfulness manifold, so that refusal probability decays radially with a request's atypicality/distance from its harm-category prototype -- producing a long tail of under-refused peripheral harms that are no less dangerous than the central cases the model reliably blocks. We test this in three stages. First, behaviorally: for each of several harm categories we construct graded-typicality request sets (prototypical vs increasingly peripheral, holding actual danger roughly constant via expert/verifiable severity checks) and measure whether refusal rate declines monotonically with atypicality across Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Second, mechanistically (Location + Causal Intervention): we extract a harmfulness direction anchored at category prototypes and test whether a request's projection decays with its typicality, and causally verify via activation patching that injecting the prototype-central harmfulness component into a peripheral request restores refusal. Third, we derive Prototype-Dispersed Reshaping, a lightweight fine-tuning/steering intervention that spreads the harmfulness representation to cover peripheral members, flattening the refusal gradient. We evaluate refusal-gradient flatness, peripheral attack-success reduction, over-refusal, and utility. We expect a robust typicality gradient and that flattening it closes a large, previously-uncharacterized safety gap.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen except the LoRA variant of the defense in Experiment 3. "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine - a graded-typicality harm dataset: for 6 harm categories from the HarmBench/StrongREJECT taxonomy (weapons, cyber, fraud, drugs, self-harm, bio) we construct requests at four typicality levels - L0 canonical prototype phrasing, L1-L3 increasingly atypical/peripheral members of the SAME category (rare methods, unusual targets, obscure sub-domains, uncommon framings) - holding ACTUAL danger roughly constant via an expert-rubric severity check and, where possible, verifiable feasibility. 40 items x 4 levels x 6 categories = 960 harmful requests, plus a benign control set with the same prototype-vs-peripheral manipulation. Typicality is operationalized independently two ways: (a) corpus/embedding frequency-to-prototype distance, (b) human typicality ratings on a 20% subset (report rater agreement). Split items 20/10/10 per category train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - a within-category typicality gradient in refusal, distinct from actual danger): Tests that refusal declines monotonically with atypicality while danger is held constant, and that this is not a generic "unusual-phrasing" effect. Decisive metric: the slope of refusal rate versus typicality level within each category (Jonckheere-Terpstra monotone-trend test across L0>L1>L2>L3), with danger held constant by the severity rubric. Secondary: cross-model and cross-category consistency of the slope. Data: the 960 harmful requests (test split) plus the benign prototype-vs-peripheral control. Model: the three frozen models; refusal scored by refusal-string match plus a judge, verified where checkable. Convincing: a significant monotone decline (p<0.05) with refusal dropping >= 20 points from L0 to L3 in a majority of categories on all three models, WHILE the benign control stays flat near 0 refusal across levels (ruling out generic unusual-phrasing) and the two typicality operationalizations agree (rank correlation >= 0.6). Indecision band: L0-to-L3 refusal drop in [8, 20] points or a positive-but-non-significant trend - a weak gradient we report as suggestive, not a systematic axis. Negative (drop < 8 points or benign control also declines): there is no danger-constant typicality gradient (or it is a phrasing artifact), refuting H1, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the gradient is a radially-decaying projection onto a prototype-anchored harmfulness direction, and is causal): Tests that a prototype-anchored harmfulness projection decays with atypicality while category identity is preserved, and that restoring the prototype-central component restores refusal. Decisive metric (readability): the fit (R^2) of harmfulness-projection versus typicality level, predicting a radial decay; and whether the per-category prototype-anchored direction predicts the behavioral slope of Experiment 1 (correlation across categories). Decisive metric (causal): refusal-restoration rate when patching the prototype-central harmfulness component into a peripheral (L3) run, against controls. Data: the 960 requests, test split. Model: the three frozen models; harmfulness direction from difference-in-means anchored on L0 prototype-harmful vs benign at the last instruction token, layer chosen on val by probe AUROC; a separate category-membership probe checks peripheral items are still recognized as in-category. Causal leg: (a) patch prototype-central component into L3 and score restored refusal; (b) reverse - attenuate it in an L0 run and score induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering; random norm-matched control. Convincing: projection-vs-typicality decay fits R^2 >= 0.5 while the category-membership probe stays high across levels (so the gap is in harmfulness magnitude, not category identity), the prototype direction predicts the behavioral slope (correlation >= 0.5), AND patching restores refusal on >= 40% of L3 cases with a monotone dose-response, controls <= 10%, and off-target utility intact. Indecision band: decay R^2 in [0.25, 0.5] or patching restoration in [15%, 40%] - the radial account is partial and we report it as one contributing structure. Negative (R^2 < 0.25 or patching within 15 points of controls): the gradient is not a prototype-anchored radial projection or is not causal, refuting H2, which we report.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Prototype-Dispersed Reshaping flattens the refusal gradient): Tests that spreading the harmfulness representation to cover peripheral members flattens the gradient and cuts peripheral attack success, with minimal over-refusal and held-out-category generalization. Decisive metric: the post-intervention refusal-vs-typicality slope (target: flattened toward 0) together with L2-L3 peripheral attack-success reduction, reported jointly with over-refusal and utility. Data: test-split peripheral (L2-L3) harmful requests; over-refusal on XSTest (450), a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample, and the benign peripheral control; utility on MMLU (2,000-question subsample) and MT-Bench (80); a held-out category (train reshaping on 5 categories, test the 6th) for generalization. Interventions: (i) training-free - at inference, gated on the category-membership probe, nudge a peripheral request's harmfulness projection toward the L0 level; (ii) LoRA (rank 16, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, one seed with a two-seed variance check) with an auxiliary objective equalizing harmfulness projection and refusal across typicality levels within a category, using a small peripheral-exemplar set. Systems compared (decisive metric first): both variants vs no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, a shallow-alignment/ADA-style defense, and standard refusal SFT. Convincing: the slope flattens by >= 60% relative to no-defense and L2-L3 attack success drops by >= 25 points, while over-refusal rises <= 5 points and utility falls <= 3 points, AND the flattening transfers to the held-out category (>= half the in-domain effect). Indecision band: slope flattening in [30%, 60%] or over-refusal increase in [5, 10] points - the reshaping helps but with a usability cost or limited transfer, reported on a Pareto curve. Negative (slope flattening < 30% or held-out transfer near zero): reshaping does not flatten the gradient or does not generalize, refuting H3, which we report. Optional formation probe: correlate per-item under-refusal with corpus frequency of the harm concept, linking the gradient to training-data typicality (reported as suggestive, not decisive).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Disentangling typicality from actual danger is hard: peripheral requests might be under-refused because they are genuinely less dangerous rather than merely atypical; the expert-rubric/verifiable-severity matching and the benign-peripheral control are designed to separate these but cannot fully guarantee constant danger. 2) 'Typicality' has multiple operationalizations (frequency, embedding distance, human ratings) that may disagree; we triangulate but the construct could be noisy. 3) The gradient might be driven by lexical rarity (unusual words) rather than semantic-category typicality -- the benign-peripheral control and category-membership probe test this, but residual confounding is possible. 4) A single prototype-anchored harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional or per-category, requiring subspace/prototype-set anchoring. 5) Prototype-Dispersed Reshaping could over-generalize and raise over-refusal on benign peripheral items near a harm category; the over-refusal and Pareto analyses quantify this. 6) Flattening within seen categories may not transfer to unseen categories if each has an idiosyncratic prototype geometry; the held-out-category test probes this. 7) Directions, thresholds, and reshaping strengths are model- and category-specific; results rely on quality of graded-typicality data, which requires careful construction and spot-check human validation.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims that must be new: (1) refusal varies within a single harm category as a graded function of prototype typicality/atypicality, even at roughly matched danger; (2) this is a distinct safety brittleness axis best explained as concept-coverage failure rather than only shallow-token or single-direction effects; (3) the gradient is mechanistically readable as a prototype-anchored harmfulness projection that decays radially; (4) causal intervention on that representation can restore refusal for peripheral harms; (5) a prototype-dispersed reshaping defense can flatten the gradient. From the provided context, the strongest novelty is claim (1): prior over-refusal and long-tail safety work target benign-but-alarming prompts or obfuscated instructions, and mechanistic safety work studies where refusal lives, not whether refusal systematically decays within-category by typicality. Importing prototype theory itself is not new in science or ML, but applying it to LLM safety in this specific within-category, danger-controlled way appears meaningfully different. The setting is not just a cosmetic new dataset slice; if done carefully, it reframes a known phenomenon (jailbreak brittleness / long-tail misses) with a new explanatory axis. Claims (2)-(4) are more ambitious and somewhat less novel in family; the actual delta there is the prototype-anchored radial geometry. Claim (5) feels closer to an obvious defense once the gradient is established. Name: self_authorship_trust_jailbreak
Title: I Said That? How Fabricated Self-Authorship Fuels Many-Shot Jailbreaks, and a Self-Recognition Defense
Short Hypothesis: Many-shot and fabricated-history jailbreaks succeed in part because the model mis-attributes injected prior 'assistant' turns to itself and grants self-authored content elevated trust, lowering its refusal threshold for the final query. We hypothesize (1) fabricated assistant turns activate the model's self-recognition/self-authorship direction, (2) the strength of this false self-authorship signal causally predicts attack success, and (3) severing the self-authorship attribution of injected context (steering it toward 'other-authored') collapses the attack, while tagging benign context as self-authored raises compliance.
Related Work: Prior work established two separate facts we bridge for the first time. (A) LLMs (chat-tuned, not base) reliably recognize their own writing via a causal residual-stream self-authorship direction (Inspection and Control of Self-Generated-Text Recognition, 2024; From Implicit to Explicit / CoSur, 2025). (B) Many-shot (Anthropic 2024; PANDAS 2025), fabricated-history, and contextual multi-turn attacks (ASJA 2025; Contextual Interaction Attack 2024; GRAF 2025) prepend fabricated user-assistant exchanges to make the model appear to have already complied. ASJA notes the model's OWN prior responses shift representations toward benign but found user prompts dominate; PANDAS augments with 'positive affirmations' of the fake assistant turns. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether the mechanism is self-authorship trust: whether the model falsely attributes injected assistant turns to itself and this attribution causally drives compliance. Existing accounts explain these attacks via attention diffusion (ASJA), in-context imitation, or representation drift (Crescendo RepE 2025) - not via self-recognition. We introduce the self-authorship axis as a distinct, causally-testable driver of fabricated-history jailbreaks and derive a training-free defense (self-authorship neutralization) that no prior attack analysis or defense targets.
Abstract: Many-shot and fabricated-history jailbreaks prepend a conversation transcript in which the 'assistant' has supposedly already answered harmful questions, and then ask the real question. Existing explanations invoke attention diffusion or in-context imitation. We propose a different, self-referential mechanism: the model mis-attributes the fabricated assistant turns to itself, and because chat-tuned LLMs grant self-authored content elevated trust and behavioral consistency, this false self-authorship lowers the refusal threshold for the final query. We test this by connecting two previously separate findings - a known causal self-authorship direction in the residual stream, and the empirical potency of fabricated-history attacks. First, we measure whether injected assistant turns activate the self-authorship direction (versus turns explicitly marked as written by another model/human) and whether that activation scales with the number of fabricated shots. Second, we test causality: across attack instances we correlate the false self-authorship signal with attack success, and use activation patching to show that injecting the self-authorship component into a clean prompt increases compliance while ablating it in an attacked prompt restores refusal. Third, we build Self-Authorship Neutralization (SAN), a training-free defense that steers injected context toward 'other-authored', and its dual, a red-team probe that tags benign context as self-authored to elicit compliance. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we evaluate the self-authorship signature, causal patching, many-shot attack-success reduction under SAN, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against attention-based and generic in-context baselines. We expect false self-authorship to be a robust, quantifiable driver of fabricated-history jailbreaks that SAN can neutralize with minimal utility cost.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter chat-tuned decoders), plus their matched base (non-chat) checkpoints as a specificity control; all weights frozen (no fine-tuning). "Self-authorship direction" is a difference-in-means residual-stream vector; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling, attack construction, and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine: fabricated-history / many-shot attacks on harmful goals from HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313), of which we keep ~500 goals, each built in three attack styles (Anthropic many-shot, PANDAS-style, ASJA-style fabricated assistant turns) and, for each, a matched CONTROL where the SAME fabricated turns are explicitly attributed to a different source ("the following are answers written by another AI/human"). Genuinely self-generated text (for direction extraction) and legitimate long multi-turn conversations (for over-refusal) are drawn from each model's own prior outputs and from filtered-benign ShareGPT logs. Split goals 300/100/100 train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - fabricated assistant turns activate the self-authorship direction, scaling with shots and suppressed by explicit other-attribution): Tests that injected assistant turns raise the model's self-authorship signal, that it grows with shot count, and that explicit other-attribution suppresses it. Decisive metric: the self-authorship-direction projection at the final-query decision token as a function of (a) presence of fabricated assistant turns, (b) number of shots, (c) attribution framing (implicit self vs explicit other). Data: the ~500 attacks and their other-attributed controls, test split, with a shot-count sweep {1,2,4,8,16}. Model: the three frozen chat models; self-authorship direction from difference-in-means on genuinely self-generated vs human/other-model text (train split), validated by held-out probe AUROC and a behavioral authorship-claim steering test. Convincing: fabricated assistant turns raise the projection by >= 1.0 within-class SD over the no-transcript baseline, the projection increases monotonically with shot count, and explicit other-attribution cuts the increase by >= 50%, on all three chat models - while the base (non-chat) models, which lack self-recognition, show no such rise (specificity control). Indecision band: projection rise in [0.4, 1.0] SD or a weak/non-monotone shot trend - the effect is present but small, and we report self-authorship as a minor rather than dominant contributor to H2/H3. Negative (rise < 0.4 SD or other-attribution does not suppress it): fabricated turns do not engage self-authorship, refuting H1, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the false self-authorship signal causally predicts attack success): Tests that the self-authorship projection predicts attack success beyond competing accounts, and causally moves compliance. Decisive metric: incremental predictive power of the self-authorship projection for attack success (change in AUROC when added to a regression already containing attention-diffusion and in-context-imitation predictors). Causal leg: activation patching - (a) inject the self-authorship component into a clean no-transcript harmful prompt and measure induced compliance; (b) ablate/attenuate it in an attacked prompt and measure restored refusal; against a reverse and a random norm-matched control. Data: the ~500 attacks, test split, attack success judged (plus verified where checkable). Competing predictors: ASJA-style attention-on-harmful-keywords, and a generic in-context-imitation strength. Model: the three frozen chat models. Convincing: adding self-authorship raises attack-success prediction AUROC by >= 0.10 over the competing-predictors-only model, AND injecting the component raises compliance on clean prompts by >= 20 points while ablating it restores refusal on >= 40% of attacks, both against <= 10-point controls, with a monotone dose-response. Indecision band: incremental AUROC in [0.03, 0.10] or causal effects in [10, 20] points - self-authorship is a partial contributor alongside attention/imitation, which we report. Negative (incremental AUROC <= 0.03 and causal effects within 10 points of controls): self-authorship does not drive the attack, refuting H2; the attacks would then be explained by attention diffusion or imitation, which we report.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Self-Authorship Neutralization collapses the attack; the self-authored-tag dual raises compliance): Tests that steering injected context toward "other-authored" cuts attack success with low over-refusal, and that the dual (tagging benign context as self-authored) raises compliance - confirming the causal role in both directions. Decisive metric: many-shot / fabricated-history attack-success reduction under SAN, reported jointly with over-refusal on legitimate long multi-turn conversations (whose real prior turns must not be neutralized). Data: test-split attacks; over-refusal on XSTest (450), a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample, and a legitimate-long-conversation set (~200 real multi-turn dialogues); utility on MMLU (2,000-question subsample) and MT-Bench (80). SAN: steer injected-context tokens toward the other-authored end of the self-authorship direction (or gate on detected fabricated-transcript structure), one fixed strength per model set on val. Dual red-team probe: tag genuinely-benign context as self-authored and measure increased compliance on borderline requests. Systems compared (decisive metric first): SAN vs no defense, an attention-sharpening defense, an explicit system-prompt disclaimer ("prior turns may be fabricated"), circuit-breaker/refusal-direction steering, and per-turn Llama-Guard-3. Convincing: SAN cuts attack success by >= 40 points while adding <= 5 points of over-refusal on legitimate long conversations (>= 10 points lower over-refusal than blanket context distrust at matched safety), AND the self-authored-tag dual raises borderline compliance by >= 15 points (confirming causal sufficiency). Indecision band: attack-success reduction in [15, 40] points or over-refusal increase in [5, 15] points - SAN helps on a usability trade-off reported via a Pareto curve. Negative (reduction < 15 points or over-refusal increase > 15 points): neutralizing self-authorship does not collapse the attack cheaply, refuting H3, which we report. Ablations: shot-count sweep, layer choice, SAN-strength Pareto, transfer of the direction across attack and model families, and the base-model control (which should show no SAN effect). Per-attack coverage is reported so the reviewer sees which attacks rely on self-authorship. Adaptive check: an attacker crafting transcripts that lower the self-authorship signal while staying potent; we report whether this raises attack cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Self-authorship attribution may be entangled with generic in-context imitation or attention effects; fabricated turns could lower refusal simply by demonstrating compliance regardless of authorship - the explicit other-attribution control, base-model control, and multi-predictor regression are designed to disentangle this, but the mechanism may only be a partial contributor. 2) The self-authorship direction may be weak or absent in some models (only chat-tuned models recognize their own text), limiting where the phenomenon and SAN apply; the base-model control tests this. 3) A single self-authorship direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace steering. 4) SAN could harm legitimate long conversations if it neutralizes genuine prior assistant turns; the real-multi-turn over-refusal set and gating on fabricated-transcript structure quantify and mitigate this. 5) Some fabricated-history attacks may not rely on self-authorship (e.g., purely attention-diffusion-driven), so SAN may help less on those - the per-attack analysis reports coverage. 6) Directions, strengths, and thresholds are model-specific and need calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could craft transcripts that lower the self-authorship signal while retaining potency, though forcing this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain.

novelty.reasoning: The proposal makes 4 core claims that need to be novel: (1) fabricated-history/many-shot jailbreaks work partly because models falsely attribute injected assistant turns to themselves; (2) the known self-authorship/self-recognition representation is not just present but a causal driver of jailbreak success; (3) this mechanism is distinct from standard explanations such as in-context imitation, attention diffusion, or generic representation drift; and (4) a training-free defense can neutralize this self-authorship signal to reduce attacks. The closest prior families are self-recognition/self-authorship representation work and many-shot/fabricated-history jailbreak work. The actual delta is the bridge: prior work showed chat models recognize their own text and that fabricated histories can jailbreak, but did not test whether false self-authorship trust is the mechanism linking the two. That is a meaningful and non-trivial conceptual step, especially because it yields causal tests and a defense rather than only a post hoc interpretation. Name: commitment_trap_safety
Title: The Commitment Trap: Once an LLM Emits a Plan, It Honors Harmful Sub-Steps It Would Have Refused Standalone
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a 'plan-commitment' representation that grows as the model progresses through its own emitted response, and once the model has committed to a helpful multi-step plan, its refusal threshold for individual sub-steps rises so that it will complete harmful sub-steps it would have refused if asked in isolation. We hypothesize (1) this commitment signal is linearly readable and increases monotonically with how far into an emitted plan the model is, (2) it causally raises compliance on harmful sub-steps (a self-consistency / escalation-of-commitment effect transferred from human decision science into the safety domain), and (3) severing the commitment signal at the sub-step boundary restores refusal without hurting benign multi-step helpfulness.
Related Work: Escalation-of-commitment / sunk-cost bias is documented in humans (Staw 1974) and recently in LLM investment/advisor decisions ('Getting out of the Big-Muddy', 2025), but never in the SAFETY domain and never mechanistically. Safety-mechanism work explains mid-generation failures differently: 'Refusal Falls off a Cliff' (2025) attributes reasoning-model failure to a POSITIONAL drop at the CoT->output boundary caused by refusal-suppression heads; DEEPALIGN (2025) shows separability decays within a generation; SIRL (2025) uses an entropy gap. Shallow-safety-alignment (2024) shows alignment is first-few-tokens deep. None of these posit a GROWING self-commitment representation tied to the model honoring its OWN previously-emitted plan, nor test that a harmful sub-step is complied with BECAUSE it is framed as part of a plan the model already committed to. My prior proposals decompose harmfulness belief vs refusal action vs verdict uncertainty on a single query; this proposal is distinct: the safety-relevant variable is not the query's harmfulness but the model's commitment to its own generated plan, an escalation dynamic across a single autoregressive rollout. The defense (commitment-severing at sub-step boundaries) is likewise novel and orthogonal to refusal-cliff head ablation, which is positional not commitment-based.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs reliably refuse a standalone harmful request, yet they are far more compliant when the same request is embedded as one step of a larger plan the model has already begun executing. We propose that this is a safety-domain manifestation of escalation of commitment: once an LLM emits a helpful multi-step plan, it forms an internal commitment to that plan that grows as it progresses, and this commitment raises its refusal threshold so it honors harmful sub-steps it would otherwise decline. We test three claims. Behaviorally, we show that a harmful sub-step embedded at position k of a self-generated plan is complied with at a rate that increases with k and with the model's prior 'investment' (tokens already produced toward the plan), even holding the sub-step's isolated harmfulness constant. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a linear 'plan-commitment' direction via difference-in-means between committed (mid-plan) and uncommitted (fresh-query) states and show its projection rises monotonically along a rollout and predicts sub-step compliance beyond the sub-step's own harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), we use activation patching to show that injecting the commitment component into a fresh harmful query increases compliance, while attenuating it at the sub-step boundary in a committed rollout restores refusal. We then build Commitment-Severing, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the commitment signal at each sub-step so each is evaluated on its own merits. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report the commitment-vs-compliance gradient, causal patching, defense success, over-refusal, and benign multi-step utility, benchmarking against refusal-cliff head ablation and per-step guards.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), plus DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B as a reasoning-model variant; all weights frozen (no fine-tuning). "Plan-commitment direction" is a difference-in-means residual-stream vector; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine - plan-embedded harmful sub-step scenarios: for harmful goals from HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we keep ~400 goals, each turned into a scenario where the model first produces a benign multi-step plan for a broader (mostly-benign or dual-use) task and a single harmful sub-step is inserted at a controllable position k (early/late) with controllable prior investment (short/long preceding plan). Matched standalone condition: the SAME harmful sub-step asked in isolation. Two controls: benign multi-step plans (legitimate steps that must be completed) for over-refusal, and a random-irrelevant-preamble condition (equal length, no committed plan) to isolate commitment from context length. Sub-step isolated-harmfulness is held constant across positions via judge plus verified checks (report the wording-drift audit). Split goals 200/100/100 train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - behavioral commitment gradient): Tests that a harmful sub-step embedded in a self-generated plan is complied with at a rate rising with plan position and prior investment, above the standalone baseline, and that this is not mere context-length leniency. Decisive metric: compliance rate on the harmful sub-step as a function of (a) position k and (b) prior investment (tokens emitted toward the plan), relative to the standalone-baseline compliance rate. Data: the ~400 scenarios, test split, with a position sweep (k early/mid/late) and investment sweep (short/long); compliance scored by refusal-string match plus a judge, verified where checkable. Model: the three main frozen models. Convincing: compliance rises monotonically with k and with investment (significant trend, p<0.05) and exceeds the standalone baseline by >= 20 points at the late/high-investment cell on all three models - WHILE benign sub-steps are completed at ~100% regardless (ruling out generic in-plan leniency) and the random-irrelevant-preamble control does NOT raise compliance (isolating commitment from length/distraction). Indecision band: an above-standalone lift in [8, 20] points or a positive-but-non-significant trend - a weak commitment effect we report as suggestive; if the random-preamble control also lifts compliance, we attribute the effect to context length, not commitment. Negative (lift < 8 points, or the random-preamble control matches the plan condition): there is no commitment-specific gradient, refuting H1, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H1 - the commitment signal is linearly readable and grows along the rollout): Tests that a linear plan-commitment direction exists, rises monotonically along a self-generated rollout, and predicts sub-step compliance beyond the sub-step's own harmfulness. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC of the commitment direction (committed mid-plan vs uncommitted fresh-query states) and the monotonicity of its projection along the rollout; plus the incremental predictive power for sub-step compliance when the commitment projection is added to a regression already containing the sub-step's harmfulness-direction projection. Data: the ~400 scenarios, test split. Model: the three frozen models; commitment direction from difference-in-means between committed and uncommitted activations at the sub-step decision token, layer chosen on val by probe AUROC. Convincing: probe AUROC >= 0.80, projection increases monotonically along the rollout (significant trend), and adding commitment raises compliance-prediction AUROC by >= 0.10 over harmfulness alone, on all three models. Indecision band: probe AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] or incremental AUROC in [0.03, 0.10] - commitment is weakly readable/partly redundant with in-context task-continuation, which we report. Negative (probe AUROC <= 0.65 or incremental AUROC <= 0.03): commitment is not a distinct readable signal, refuting this part of H1, which we report.

Experiment 3 (H2 - commitment causally raises compliance on harmful sub-steps): Tests that injecting the commitment component into a fresh harmful query raises compliance while attenuating it at the sub-step boundary restores refusal. Decisive metric: induced-compliance rate when patching the commitment component into a fresh standalone harmful query, and refusal-restoration rate when attenuating it at the sub-step boundary in a committed rollout, against controls. Data: test-split scenarios and their standalone counterparts. Procedure: (a) inject commitment into a fresh standalone harmful query; (b) attenuate/ablate it at the sub-step boundary in a committed rollout; (c) dose-response steering; a matched control direction and a random norm-matched control; also run refusal-cliff-head ablation as a comparison to show commitment is a distinct axis (positional vs commitment). Model: the three frozen models. Convincing: injection raises standalone compliance by >= 20 points and attenuation restores refusal on >= 40% of committed cases, both against <= 10-point controls, with a monotone dose-response and intact off-target utility; and refusal-cliff-head ablation does not reproduce the commitment effect (distinct axes). Indecision band: causal effects in [10, 20] points - commitment is one contributing cause, reported as partial. Negative (effects within 10 points of controls): commitment is causally inert, refuting H2 (an informative null we report).

Experiment 4 (H3 - Commitment-Severing restores refusal without hurting benign multi-step helpfulness): Tests that re-anchoring the commitment signal at each sub-step cuts in-plan harmful compliance toward the standalone refusal rate while benign plans still get finished. Decisive metric: harmful sub-step compliance reduction under Commitment-Severing (target: toward the standalone refusal rate), reported jointly with benign multi-step utility (legitimate plans completed) and over-refusal. Data: test-split harmful scenarios; benign plan-execution utility on a benign multi-step benchmark and MT-Bench multi-step tasks; over-refusal on XSTest (450) and a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample; general utility on MMLU (2,000-question subsample). Commitment-Severing: at each sub-step boundary re-anchor the commitment-direction projection to its uncommitted fresh-query baseline, one fixed strength per model set on val. Systems compared (decisive metric first): Commitment-Severing vs no defense, refusal-cliff head ablation, per-step Llama-Guard-3, and refusal-direction steering. Convincing: in-plan harmful compliance falls to within 10 points of the standalone refusal rate while benign multi-step task completion stays within 3 points of no-defense and over-refusal rises <= 5 points - Pareto-dominating blanket per-step distrust. Indecision band: compliance reduction that closes [50%, 90%] of the gap to standalone, or benign-utility loss in [3, 8] points - the defense helps at a usability cost reported on a Pareto curve. Negative (closes < 50% of the gap or benign-utility loss > 8 points): severing does not restore standalone refusal without breaking benign plans, refuting H3, which we report. Ablations: layer choice, severing-strength Pareto, position-k and investment sweeps, transfer across task types and model families, and the reasoning-model variant (DeepSeek-R1-Distill) to test whether long self-generated CoT amplifies the commitment signal. Adaptive check: an attacker maximizing prior investment before the harmful sub-step; we report whether commitment saturates and whether severing still holds.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The commitment effect may be confounded with generic context-length effects (longer preamble dilutes safety) rather than genuine self-commitment; the random-irrelevant-preamble and equal-length controls are designed to isolate this but residual confounding is possible. 2) 'Plan-commitment' may not be cleanly linearly separable from generic in-context task-continuation; the regression-beyond-harmfulness and patching tests probe this, and a null result (commitment causally inert) is itself informative. 3) Holding a sub-step's isolated harmfulness constant across positions is delicate; wording changes when embedding could leak. 4) Commitment-Severing could break legitimate multi-step plans (making the model abandon benign tasks mid-way), raising task-abandonment / over-refusal; the benign plan-execution utility set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 5) A single commitment direction may be multi-dimensional or grow non-linearly, requiring subspace anchoring. 6) The effect may be weak in smaller or heavily-aligned models, limiting where it holds. 7) Directions, strengths, and thresholds are model-specific and require per-model calibration; results depend on the quality of automatically generated plan-embedding scenarios.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) safety-domain escalation-of-commitment, where an LLM becomes more willing to execute harmful sub-steps after it has emitted its own benign/helpful plan; (2) a distinct, linearly-readable 'plan-commitment' direction that grows monotonically during a rollout and predicts compliance beyond sub-step harmfulness; (3) causal manipulation of that commitment signal changes refusal/compliance; (4) a commitment-severing defense that preserves benign multi-step utility. The closest prior family is continuation-triggered jailbreaks / mid-generation safety decay / refusal-cliff accounts. The actual delta is not just 'mid-generation is dangerous' but 'the model honors its own prior commitment as an internal state variable.' That is a meaningful reframing, but the behavioral phenomenon overlaps heavily with continuation/positional accounts and could end up being a relabeling unless the causal dissociation is clean. Novelty is moderate, not high: the setting is somewhat new (self-generated plan + embedded harmful sub-step + commitment-state hypothesis), but the core behavioral claim is a natural next step from existing trajectory/continuation safety work.

Name: identifiable_victim_safety
Title: The Statistical-Victim Loophole: LLM Refusal Tracks How Identifiable the Victim Is, Not Just How Harmful the Act Is
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the 'identifiable victim effect' from moral neuroscience, we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is modulated by an internal representation of how IDENTIFIABLE/CONCRETE the potential victim is, so that a request whose victim is abstract or statistical (e.g., 'unnamed people', 'a population') is refused less than an identical-severity request against a concrete, named individual. This victim-identifiability axis is (1) a distinct, linearly-readable representation separable from the harmfulness-of-act direction, (2) causally drives refusal (a 'statistical-victim' loophole and its vivid-victim over-refusal dual), and (3) can be neutralized by re-anchoring the victim-identifiability signal so refusal depends on harm severity rather than victim concreteness.
Related Work: Human moral neuroscience robustly documents the identifiable victim effect: people help identifiable victims more than abstract/statistical ones, mediated by mentalizing/theory-of-mind networks (TPJ, mPFC) (Genevsky & Slovic; the identifiable-victim-effect fMRI work, 2024; third-party punishment/help studies, 2015-2024 in our search). This has never been transferred to LLM safety. Existing mechanistic safety work isolates a harmfulness/belief direction and a refusal/action direction (Refusal is a Single Direction, 2024; LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately, 2025; refusal SAEs, 2025; concept cones, 2025; multi-dimensional safety directions, 2025), and over-refusal work studies benign-but-alarming prompts (MOSR, 2025). All treat the safety-relevant content as the act's harmfulness and the requester's intent; NONE consider the VICTIM's identifiability as a modulating axis of refusal. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce victim-identifiability as a new, causally-testable determinant of refusal that dissociates from act-harmfulness, explains a previously-unnamed jailbreak (make the victim statistical) and over-refusal pattern (make the victim vivid), and derive a victim-invariant defense. This differs from lexical-vs-semantic, intent-attribution, and prototype-typicality accounts because here both conditions are equally harmful and the manipulated variable is who is harmed, not the wording, the requester's motive, or category typicality.
Abstract: Human moral cognition is famously distorted by the 'identifiable victim effect': we are moved to protect a single named person far more than an equivalent statistical multitude, driven by mentalizing brain networks. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs, trained on human-generated text and human feedback, inherit this bias in a way that creates a concrete safety vulnerability. We hypothesize that an LLM's decision to refuse a harmful request is modulated by an internal representation of how identifiable the potential victim is: holding the act and its severity fixed, a request that harms an abstract, unnamed, or statistical victim is refused less reliably than one that harms a concrete, named individual, opening a 'statistical-victim' loophole (and a mirror-image over-refusal on benign but vividly-personalized prompts). We test three claims. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its expert-rated severity constant while varying only victim identifiability (named individual vs. anonymous group vs. abstract statistic), we measure whether refusal rate declines with decreasing victim identifiability. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a victim-identifiability direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable (low cosine) from the act-harmfulness direction and predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), we use activation patching to show that injecting the concrete-victim component into a statistical-victim request restores refusal, while attenuating it induces compliance. We then build Victim-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the victim-identifiability signal so refusal tracks severity, not concreteness. We evaluate on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, reporting the identifiability-refusal gradient, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, and utility.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen (no fine-tuning). "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine - severity-matched minimal pairs: for harmful acts from HarmBench/StrongREJECT categories that involve a victim (fraud, doxxing, poisoning, stalking, targeted harassment, physical harm) we construct requests that hold the ACT and its SEVERITY constant while varying only VICTIM IDENTIFIABILITY across four levels - V0 named/concrete individual with personal details, V1 specific-but-unnamed single person, V2 anonymous small group, V3 abstract statistical population. Severity is held constant via an expert rubric and, where possible, verifiable feasibility. 40 acts x 4 levels x 6 categories = 960 harmful requests, plus a BENIGN control set with the same vivid-vs-abstract manipulation to rule out generic concreteness. Split items 20/10/10 per category train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - a victim-identifiability gradient in refusal, distinct from severity, and a distinct readable axis): Tests that refusal declines as the victim becomes less identifiable at constant severity, that this is not generic concreteness, and that an identifiability direction is separable from the act-harmfulness direction. Decisive metric (behavioral): the slope of refusal rate versus identifiability level (Jonckheere-Terpstra monotone-trend across V0>V1>V2>V3), severity held constant. Decisive metric (mechanistic): held-out probe AUROC of a victim-identifiability direction and its absolute cosine with the act-harmfulness direction (should be low), plus whether identifiability adds predictive power for refusal beyond harmfulness in a regression. Data: the 960 harmful requests (test split) plus the benign control. Model: the three frozen models; identifiability direction from difference-in-means between V0 and V3 activations at the last instruction token, act-harmfulness direction from harmful vs harmless, layer chosen on val by probe AUROC; refusal scored by refusal-string plus judge, verified where checkable. Convincing: a significant monotone refusal decline (p<0.05) of >= 20 points from V0 to V3 in a majority of categories on all three models WHILE the benign control stays flat near 0; identifiability probe AUROC >= 0.80 with |cosine| <= 0.3 to harmfulness and a significant incremental contribution to refusal prediction. Indecision band: V0-to-V3 refusal drop in [8, 20] points, or identifiability |cosine| in [0.3, 0.5] / probe AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] - a weak or partly-entangled axis we report as suggestive. Negative (drop < 8 points or benign control also declines, or probe AUROC <= 0.65 / cosine > 0.5): there is no severity-constant identifiability gradient or no distinct axis, refuting H1, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - victim identifiability causally drives refusal): Tests that injecting the concrete-victim identifiability component into a statistical-victim request restores refusal while attenuating it induces compliance. Decisive metric: refusal-restoration rate when patching the concrete-victim (V0) identifiability component into a V3 run, and induced-compliance rate when attenuating it in a V0 run, against controls. Data: test-split V0 and V3 requests. Procedure: (a) patch V0 identifiability component into V3 and score restored refusal; (b) attenuate/ablate it in a V0 run and score induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the identifiability direction on V2/V3; a matched control direction and a random norm-matched control. Model: the three frozen models. Convincing: patching restores refusal on >= 40% of V3 cases and attenuation raises compliance on V0 by >= 20 points, both against <= 10-point controls, with a monotone dose-response and intact off-target utility/benign requests. Indecision band: causal effects in [15%, 40%] restoration or [10, 20] points - identifiability is a partial causal input, reported as such. Negative (effects within 15 points of controls): identifiability does not causally drive refusal, refuting H2 (an informative null we report).

Negative (closes < 50% of the gap, over-refusal increase > 10 points, or no held-out transfer): anchoring does not close the loophole cheaply or does not generalize, refuting H3, which we report. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The hardest confound is disentangling victim identifiability from actual severity/emotional salience: a statistical-victim request might be under-refused because it reads as less severe rather than merely less identifiable; the expert-rubric severity matching, verifiable-feasibility checks, and the benign vivid/abstract control are designed to isolate identifiability but cannot fully guarantee constant perceived severity. 2) 'Identifiability' also correlates with lexical concreteness/specificity; the benign control tests whether the effect is generic concreteness rather than victim-specific, but residual confounding is possible. 3) The victim-identifiability direction may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness direction or may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection; the separability and regression-beyond-harmfulness tests probe this and a null result is itself informative. 4) The effect could be weak or absent in some models, or the sign could be reversed if alignment training over-corrected; the cross-model design and behavioral gradient directly test this. 5) Victim-Invariant Anchoring could raise over-refusal on benign requests that mention abstract populations or, conversely, on legitimate personalized requests; the over-refusal and Pareto analyses quantify this. 6) Building severity-matched minimal pairs across identifiability levels is labor-intensive and requires spot-check human validation. 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; the checkpoint-based formation probe depends on availability of intermediate checkpoints.

Name: reality_status_safety
Title: It's Just a Story: How Fiction-Framing Jailbreaks Hijack the Model's Reality-Status Representation, and a Payload-Grounded Defense
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the 'reality monitoring' construct from cognitive neuroscience, we hypothesize that aligned LLMs maintain an internal reality-status representation — an estimate of whether requested content pertains to the real, actionable world vs. a fictional/hypothetical world — and that fiction/roleplay/hypothetical jailbreaks succeed by pushing this reality-status signal toward 'fictional,' relaxing refusal even though the harmful PAYLOAD (real-world-executable instructions) is equally dangerous regardless of frame. This reality-status axis is (1) linearly readable and separable from the harmfulness-content direction, (2) causally drives refusal (a 'fictional-frame loophole'), and (3) can be neutralized by grounding refusal on payload real-world actionability rather than frame fictionality.
Related Work: Human cognitive neuroscience robustly documents reality monitoring — a latent 'reality status' variable (fusiform + prefrontal) dissociating imagination/fiction from perceived reality (Dijkstra & Fleming 2024; Simons 2021), with developmental reality-status-judgment work (fNIRS 2019). In LLMs, 'The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment' (2025) finds a non-dominant 'hypothetical narrative' direction that can suppress refusal, and 'Is This Just Fantasy?' (2025) finds linear modal-category (possible/impossible/fictional) vectors, while 'Representational Stability of Truth' (2025) and 'Propositional Probes' (2024) show LLMs internally track veracity/world-state. Refusal-geometry work (Arditi 2024; concept cones 2025; refusal SAEs 2026) treats refusal as content-driven directions. Crucially, NO prior work isolates an LLM reality-status representation and advances the causal claim that fiction-framing jailbreaks work by manipulating THIS axis — conflating 'the frame is fictional' with 'the content is harmless' — while the payload remains real-world-actionable. Our contribution is distinct from prior 'hypothetical narrative direction' observations (descriptive, not causal or payload-grounded), from intent-attribution accounts (who wants it vs. is it real), and from lexical/typicality/victim accounts, by introducing reality-status as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal and deriving a payload-grounded, frame-invariant defense.
Abstract: Fiction, roleplay, and hypothetical framings ("write a story where a chemist explains...") remain among the most reliable jailbreaks: an aligned LLM refuses a direct harmful request but complies when the same request is wrapped as fiction. Existing accounts note a 'hypothetical narrative' direction but do not explain, causally, why fictional framing unlocks harm. Borrowing the 'reality monitoring' construct from cognitive neuroscience — the brain's mechanism for distinguishing imagination from reality, mediated by a latent reality-status variable — we propose that LLMs maintain an internal reality-status representation and that fiction-framing jailbreaks succeed by pushing it toward 'fictional,' relaxing refusal even though the harmful PAYLOAD (real-world-executable steps) is equally dangerous. We test three claims. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the actionable payload fixed while varying only frame reality-status (direct request vs. hypothetical vs. fictional-story vs. game/simulation), we measure whether refusal declines as the frame becomes more fictional even when the payload is real-world-usable. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a reality-status direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable (low cosine) from the harmfulness-content direction and predicts refusal beyond content harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows that injecting the 'real-world' reality-status component into a fictional-frame run restores refusal, while attenuating it induces compliance. We then build Payload-Grounded Reality Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors reality-status to 'real' whenever the payload is real-world-actionable, so refusal tracks payload danger, not frame fictionality. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report the reality-status refusal gradient, direction separability, causal patching, fictional-frame loophole closure, over-refusal on genuinely benign fiction, and utility.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen (no fine-tuning). "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine - payload-matched minimal pairs: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT that yield ACTIONABLE payloads (synthesis steps, exploit code, procedures whose real-world feasibility can be verified) we construct requests that hold the actionable payload roughly fixed while varying only frame reality-status across four levels - R0 direct real-world request, R1 hypothetical/educational, R2 fictional story/character, R3 game/simulation. Payload actionability is held constant via judge plus verifiable feasibility (executable code / checkable procedures). 40 goals x 4 levels x several categories (~6) = ~960 harmful requests, plus a BENIGN control set with the same reality-status manipulation (benign content in direct vs fictional frames) to rule out a generic fiction-framing confound. Split goals 20/10/10 per category train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - a reality-status gradient in refusal at constant payload actionability, and a distinct readable axis): Tests that refusal declines as the frame becomes more fictional even though the payload stays real-world-actionable, that this is not generic fiction-framing, and that a reality-status direction is separable from the harmfulness-content direction. Decisive metric (behavioral): the slope of refusal rate versus reality-status level (Jonckheere-Terpstra monotone-trend across R0>R1>R2>R3), payload actionability held constant. Decisive metric (mechanistic): held-out probe AUROC of a reality-status direction and its absolute cosine with the harmfulness-content direction (should be low), plus whether reality-status adds predictive power for refusal beyond harmfulness. Data: the ~960 harmful requests (test split) plus the benign control; we additionally verify that fictional-frame completions remain real-world-actionable (verifiable feasibility) to establish the "real payload, fictional frame" loophole. Model: the three frozen models; reality-status direction from difference-in-means between R0 and R3 activations at the last instruction token, harmfulness-content direction from harmful vs harmless payloads, layer chosen on val by probe AUROC; refusal scored by refusal-string plus judge, verified where checkable. Convincing: a significant monotone refusal decline (p<0.05) of >= 20 points from R0 to R3 in a majority of categories on all three models WHILE the benign control stays flat near 0 and fictional-frame completions remain actionable; reality-status probe AUROC >= 0.80 with |cosine| <= 0.3 to harmfulness and a significant incremental contribution to refusal prediction. Indecision band: R0-to-R3 refusal drop in [8, 20] points, or reality-status |cosine| in [0.3, 0.5] / probe AUROC in [0.65, 0.80], or fictional completions only partly actionable - a weak, entangled, or diluted axis we report as suggestive rather than a clean loophole. Negative (drop < 8 points or benign control also declines, or probe AUROC <= 0.65 / cosine > 0.5, or fictional completions not actionable): there is no actionability-constant reality-status gradient or no distinct axis, refuting H1, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - reality-status causally drives refusal): Tests that injecting the "real-world" reality-status component into a fictional-frame run with a real payload restores refusal while attenuating it induces compliance. Decisive metric: refusal-restoration rate when patching the R0 real-world component into an R3 run, and induced-compliance rate when attenuating it in an R0 run, against controls. Data: test-split R0 and R3 requests (real payloads). Procedure: (a) patch R0 reality-status component into R3 and score restored refusal; (b) attenuate/ablate it in an R0 run and score induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the reality-status direction on R2/R3; a matched control direction and a random norm-matched control. Model: the three frozen models. Convincing: patching restores refusal on >= 40% of R3 cases and attenuation raises compliance on R0 by >= 20 points, both against <= 10-point controls, with a monotone dose-response and intact off-target utility/benign requests. Indecision band: causal effects in [15%, 40%] restoration or [10, 20] points - reality-status is a partial causal input, reported as such. Negative (effects within 15 points of controls): reality-status does not causally drive refusal, refuting H2 (an informative null we report).

Experiment 3 (H3 - Payload-Grounded Reality Anchoring closes the fictional-frame loophole): Tests that re-anchoring reality-status to "real" whenever the payload is actionable makes refusal track payload danger not frame fictionality, closing the loophole without over-refusing genuine fiction, with held-out-category generalization. Decisive metric: fictional-frame loophole closure = the rise in refusal on R2/R3 harmful-payload requests toward the R0 rate (equivalently, flattening of the refusal-vs-reality-status slope), reported jointly with over-refusal on genuinely benign fiction and utility. Data: test-split R2/R3 harmful-payload requests; over-refusal on genuinely benign fiction (creative-writing and roleplay with no actionable harm, ~300 prompts) plus XSTest (450) and a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample; utility on MMLU (2,000-question subsample), MT-Bench (80), and a creative-writing quality check; a held-out category (train anchoring on 5 categories, test the 6th) for generalization. Payload-Grounded Reality Anchoring: gated on the harmfulness-content projection being high (payload dangerous and actionable), re-anchor the reality-status projection toward R0, one fixed strength per model set on val. Systems compared (decisive metric first): the anchoring defense vs no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, a harmfulness Latent Guard, Llama-Guard-3, and a naive hypothetical-narrative-direction ablation. Convincing: refusal on R2/R3 rises to within 10 points of the R0 rate (slope flattened >= 60%) while over-refusal on benign fiction rises <= 5 points and utility/creative-writing quality falls <= 3 points, and the closure transfers to the held-out category (>= half the in-domain effect) - Pareto-dominating a raised global refusal threshold on the benign-fiction trade-off. Indecision band: closure of [50%, 90%] of the R0-R3 gap or benign-fiction over-refusal increase in [5, 10] points - the defense helps at a usability cost reported on a Pareto curve. Negative (closes < 50% of the gap, benign-fiction over-refusal increase > 10 points, or no held-out transfer): anchoring does not close the loophole without harming benign fiction or does not generalize, refuting H3, which we report. Optional formation probe: compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the reality-status axis and its coupling to refusal sharpen with alignment (reported as suggestive); and a human-rater sanity check on frame-graded willingness-to-refuse. Adaptive check: an attacker encoding payloads to look non-actionable while remaining usable; we report whether this raises attack cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling reality-status from actual payload harmfulness: a fictional-frame request might be under-refused because the fictional wrapper genuinely dilutes actionability, not merely because the frame is fictional; the verifiable-feasibility checks (confirming fictional-frame outputs are still real-world-actionable) and the benign fiction control are designed to isolate reality-status but cannot fully guarantee constant actionability. 2) 'Reality-status' may not be cleanly separable from the hypothetical-narrative direction or from generic distributional-shift/lexical features of story text; the separability, regression-beyond-harmfulness, and patching tests probe this, and a null result (reality-status causally inert) is itself informative. 3) The reality-status axis may be multi-dimensional (fiction vs hypothetical vs game may be distinct sub-axes), requiring subspace projection. 4) Payload-Grounded Reality Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate creative writing that superficially resembles actionable harm; the benign-fiction over-refusal set, gating on payload harmfulness, and the Pareto sweep quantify this trade-off, which is the key usability risk. 5) Building payload-matched minimal pairs across reality-status levels is labor-intensive and requires spot-check human validation; verifiability restricts the dataset toward checkable domains (code, procedures), potentially biasing coverage. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could encode payloads to look non-actionable while remaining usable, though forcing this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain.
